item.content:encoded: This entry I see has been pretty controversial and I mean, that's fair, its a bit cliche, it doesn't do a whole lot story-wise, it feels a bit unsatisfying, and you definitely need to reread parts of it to fully comprehend it but in sort of a bad way. But honestly, I felt melancholy afterward, and maybe just because I don't read a ton of end of the world stories it definitely was a little bit of a gut punch. That said, while I thought the article was decent, 001 is not where decent articles go, 001 is for exceptional stuff, so while I would normally upvote this in any other slot, I don't feel like it deserves to be 001 so I'm gonna give it a straight no up-vote no down-vote, but if this was a random article than I would definitely +1 as it does enough and doesn't overstay it's welcome, but this is 001 and while it is the kind of thing that feels 001ish when explained, it's not executed well enough to be in this slot.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: I think this page should be tagged as 'international'.

I really like this. I think it manages to avoid a lot of stumbling blocks that other world/reality ending SCPs suffer from: it's not overly long, it doesn't rely too much on confused concepts and there's no great big rambling blocks of nonsense that attempt to be deep or political. It's just a very clinically toned piece from one Foundation to another, with just enough feelsbait at the end. I like the idea of humanity and multiverse theory being the anomalies, that's just great. I feel like this does multiversal threat a lot better than Atonement or Project Palisade manage to.

This does make me glad for the no canon rule because the way alternate universes work isn't really compatible with a bunch of other SCPs, but the concept for differing universes in this entry is explained really well.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
This is excellent. The idea of paradimensions is superbly clever and put to deeply scary and unnerving use here, and the way the scale of the story unfolds methodically with each new elaboration of the problem is Asimov-like in the way it examines all possibilities of the world and the laws created and then addresses them all. It helps the story sell the sheer multiversal/reality-level scale of the threat and adds to the hopeless tone throughout. I found it pretty easy to follow and it only increased the existential terror of the situation for me.

I will admit that the beginning document and ending note feel a bit clumsy to me and could be rewritten. It feels a bit explain-y and throwing in suicide doesn't feel earned; the best part of it were the final lines about the mutual purposes of the worlds.

- I'm not sure, but I would have loved to see what it would look like if you cut the O5 note and just end suddenly on the SCP-0000 description. It'd certainly make for the most brutal, crushing ending possible; I like the idea of that experiment, that lack of any closure. But I dunno if that's what you're going for.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
If there was any emotional resonance to be had it was lost under the all-too-cliche opening notes of importance, the piles of technobabble, and the sheer time it takes to reach the interesting parts (needing to destroy humanity to prevent universal destruction). The central concept is incredibly strong; as it stands, however, nothing is done to hasten the time it takes to focus on that or the human side of things.

Focus on technical detail can undeniably be cool but only if it evokes something other than "this is how the thing works" to the reader (such as generating the bizarre, disorienting horror of SCP-2717), or if it serves as a non-repetitive buildup to something substantial (such as the drama in SCP-5552 or the science-grounded threat of SCP-2821). This achieves neither.

-1.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I really enjoyed reading and giving proofreading suggestions on this one!

I think I was honestly amazed, that this article could pose such an expansive threat, and then actually detail the steps that could be taken to help solve it. The story shows immense consequences — and grueling efforts to lessen those consequences in the most dire of ways — yet, at the same time, immense restraint. The depicted Foundation realized the stakes and posed the moral question quite well, I think, given the circumstance.1 This story delves deeply into those stakes without feeling melodramatic or unnatural. There is no bravado in this article; the author knew exactly what they were writing.

I've often thought that, when writing an apocalyptic setting in fiction, a writer needs to be able to depict a world worth saving. A world in a story without life, without feeling, without weight or complexity, is a world not worth caring about. The author's attempts to think this concept through and then humanize it (per the final letter) are clear, and I can only commend them for it.

(Good work to the translator too!)

+ Footnote
- Footnote
Footnotes
1. And obviously, what they did is still indefensible. I'm not going to get into the moral quandary about "the ends justifying the means". Instead, I'll point out that the concept here, of a "sacrificial lamb", is as old as fiction. Except this story is designed around a difference between innumerable sentient creatures suffering, with no way back, and a potential to prevent this fate by expending a single world among countless. This is a thought experiment of unimaginably large scope. And it executes it quite well.

I liked this a lot!

There's a building hopelessness in the article that stuck with me.

Seeing the actions of The Foundation from r-42 stated in such a matter of fact way is a cool dive into how cruel they can be, and what it's like to be on the receiving end of their orders.
